title: Supreme Court orders Rs 30 lakh for man kept in jail seven years after his acquittal
dek: Chhattisgarh never acted on a 2018 High Court order freeing him. The court blamed 'institutional dysfunction' and noted that India still has no law on compensation for wrongful imprisonment.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Supreme Court has ordered the Chhattisgarh government to pay Rs 30 lakh to a man who stayed in prison for more than seven years after the state's High Court had acquitted him of murder, and has pointed out that India still has no law setting out how victims of wrongful imprisonment should be compensated.

A bench of Justices Augustine George Masih and Sanjeev Sachdeva said on Monday that the detention violated the man's right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution, and blamed what it called "institutional dysfunction" and "complete remissness" on the part of every authority involved, according to reports of the judgment. The state must pay within four weeks, after adjusting any amount the High Court has already awarded.

## What happened

The man was arrested in December 2012 in a murder case and sentenced to life imprisonment by a sessions court in August 2013. The Chhattisgarh High Court set aside his conviction on 20 January 2018, and the state did not appeal, so the acquittal became final. But he was released only on 19 May 2025, after seven years, three months and 21 days of what the Supreme Court called illegal detention.

The state blamed a communication gap between the jail and legal aid officials, according to reports. The court noted that the jail superintendent had written in 2018 asking about the status of the appeal and received no reply. The man had "lost his prime youth on account of the apathy" of the authorities, the bench said, describing Rs 30 lakh as "the bare minimum required to meaningfully redress the wrong" and saying the award was redress, not charity.

## A gap in the law

The judgment relies on a 2017 Delhi High Court ruling, Babloo Chauhan, and the Law Commission's 277th report, on wrongful prosecution, both of which recognised that wrongful imprisonment causes financial ruin, stigma and psychological trauma. The Law Commission recommended in 2018 that Parliament create a legal framework for compensating people who are wrongly prosecuted or jailed; no such law has been passed, so victims depend on case-by-case court decisions.

Instead of directing Parliament, the bench asked High Courts to consider issuing guidelines like those framed by the Madhya Pradesh High Court after a Supreme Court ruling in September 2025, which awarded Rs 25 lakh to a man kept in jail after he had finished his sentence. It also asked High Courts to consider setting up an online system, modelled on Madhya Pradesh's, that links courts and prisons so that release orders reach jails promptly.

## Other orders on Monday

The Supreme Court also allowed the National Investigation Agency to move cases over the November 2025 car-bomb explosion near the Red Fort in Delhi from Jammu and Kashmir and Haryana to the special NIA court at Patiala House in Delhi, where the three cases will be tried together, according to reports. The agency argued that they formed one "larger conspiracy" with overlapping accused and evidence.

In a separate order on the Yamuna, uploaded on Monday, a bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Manmohan warned that states and Union territories through which the river flows could face financial penalties, saying "the quality of water leaving a State should not be worse than when it entered that State". It directed the Central Pollution Control Board to monitor water quality where the river crosses state and district boundaries and to carry out surprise checks of sewage treatment plants, and listed the case for 13 January 2027.

## What happens next

Chhattisgarh has four weeks to pay. Whether other High Courts follow the Madhya Pradesh model is up to them; a national compensation law would need Parliament to act.
